title: Reframing Interaction Design Basics
intro: Academic definitions of interaction design laws are technically correct and practically useless in a design review. Calabro reframes eight of them in plain language.

learn.title: Six laws, reframed
learn.text:
**Fitts's Law** — put things near the user's cursor; make the important things bigger.
**Law of Magic Pixels** — users look in corners and can reach them easily. Use corners for global elements.
**Hick's Law** — break things into categories and steps when they get complicated.
**Progressive Disclosure** — show users what they need, when they need it.
**Miller's Law** — don't make users remember things or think too hard.
**Affordances & Signifiers** — make it look like what it does; tell users what will happen.

try.q: Which is the plain reframe of Miller's Law that Calabro teaches?
options: Don't make users remember things
Keep every menu to seven items
Show seven options, then paginate
Group related options into chunks of five to nine
try.explain: He explicitly says it is not about the magic number seven.

left.label: Academic version
items: Time to acquire a target ∝ distance ÷ size
Decision time increases with the number of choices

right.label: Plain reframe
items: Put it near the cursor; make it bigger
Break it into categories and steps
Don't make users remember or think hard

learn.title: The two that seem to contradict
learn.text:
Fitts's Law says put things near the predicted cursor. The Law of Magic Pixels says users head for the corners. Which wins?

**Context decides.** Use corners for global elements — navigation, logout, settings. Place contextual elements near the thing being acted on.

try.q: Where does a global “Log out” control belong, by these two laws?
options: In a corner
Next to the user's current cursor position
Centred at the bottom of the page
Wherever the design system happens to place it
try.explain: Corners for global elements; near the cursor for contextual ones.

learn.title: Jakob's Law overrides the rest
learn.text:
Jakob's Law — users spend more time on other sites than yours, so leverage familiar patterns — is the **guiding principle that overlays all the others**.

When in doubt, default to what users already expect.

Why reframe at all? Academic language starts a theoretical discussion. Plain language produces a design decision.

try.q: Two laws point to different solutions and the team is stuck. What does Calabro suggest?
options: Default to the familiar pattern
Apply whichever law was published earliest
Run an A/B test on both versions
Escalate the decision to the product manager
try.explain: He calls Jakob's Law the overriding principle.

test.q: Why does Calabro reframe the laws in plain language?
options: Plain language produces design decisions
Academic definitions are factually wrong
Junior designers don't read research papers
Plain language is required by most design systems
test.explain: Academic phrasing activates theoretical discussion instead.

test.q: What does the Law of Magic Pixels describe?
options: Users look for things in corners and reach them easily
Screens have a fixed number of usable pixels
Users notice movement before they notice colour
Magic numbers in layout grids improve scanning

test.q: Which law is the reframe “show users what they need when they need it”?
options: Progressive disclosure
Hick's Law
Fitts's Law
The aesthetic-usability effect

test.q: Hick's Law, in Calabro's reframe, tells you to:
options: Break complicated things into categories and steps
Remove at least half of the options
Limit menus to a maximum of seven items
Put the most popular option first in every list
test.explain: It is about reducing decision load, not deleting content.

test.q: What is the difference between an affordance and a signifier?
options: It looks like what it does vs. it says what will happen
One is visual and one is written in the code
One applies to desktop and one to mobile devices
Affordances are tested; signifiers are decided by the brand
test.explain: Affordance: can I interact? Signifier: what happens if I do?
